documents.title: RFC 6797 excerpt
documents.text: HTTP [RFC2616] may be used over various transports, typically the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP). Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. However, TCP does not provide channel integrity protection, confidentiality, or secure host identification. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. Thus, the Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) protocol [RFC6101] and its successor, Transport Layer Security (TLS) [RFC5246] were developed in order to provide channel-oriented security and are typically layered between application protocols and TCP. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. [RFC2818] specifies how HTTP is layered onto TLS and defines the Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) scheme of "https" (in practice, however, HTTP user agents (UAs) typically use either TLS or SSL3, depending upon a combination of negotiation with the server and user preferences).

documents.text: Note: This document cannot assess the probability or the risk associated with a particular threat because those aspects strongly depend on the particular application and deployment OAuth is used to protect. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. Similarly, impacts are given on a rather abstract level. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. But the information given here may serve as a foundation for deployment-specific threat models. Implementors may refine and detail the abstract threat model in order to account for the specific properties of their deployment and to come up with a risk analysis. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. As this document is based on the base OAuth 2.0 specification, it does not consider proposed extensions such as client registration or discovery, many of which are still under discussion.

documents.title: RFC 6943 excerpt
documents.text: Second, some strings are visually confusable with others, and hence if a security decision is made by a user based on visual inspection, many opportunities for false positives exist. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. As such, using visual inspection for security is unreliable. In addition to the security issues, visual confusability also adversely affects the usability of identifiers distributed via visual media. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. Similar issues can arise with audible confusability when using audio (e.g., for radio distribution, accessibility to the blind, etc.) in place of a visual medium. Furthermore, when strings conflate two types of identifiers as discussed in Section 4.1, allowing non-ASCII characters can cause one type of identifier to appear to a human as another type of identifier. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. For example, characters that may look like digits and dots may appear to be an IPv4 literal to a human (especially to one who might expect digits to appear in his or her native script). Hence, conflation often increases the chance of confusability.

documents.title: RFC 6961 excerpt
documents.text: If the OCSP response received from the server does not result in a definite "good" or "revoked" status, it is inconclusive. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. A TLS client in such a case MAY check the validity of the server certificate through other means, e.g., by directly querying the certificate issuer. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. If such processing still results in an inconclusive response, then the application using the TLS connection will have to decide whether to close the connection or not. documents.title: RFC 6962 excerpt
documents.text: Logs MUST verify that the submitted end-entity certificate or Precertificate has a valid signature chain leading back to a trusted root CA certificate, using the chain of intermediate CA certificates provided by the submitter. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. Logs MAY accept certificates that have expired, are not yet valid, have been revoked, or are otherwise not fully valid according to X.509 verification rules in order to accommodate quirks of CA certificate-issuing software. However, logs MUST refuse to publish certificates without a valid chain to a known root CA. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. If a certificate is accepted and an SCT issued, the accepting log MUST store the entire chain used for verification, including the certificate or Precertificate itself and including the root certificate used to verify the chain (even if it was omitted from the submission), and MUST present this chain for auditing upon request. This chain is required to prevent a CA from avoiding blame by logging a partial or empty chain. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. (Note: This effectively excludes self-signed and DANE-based certificates until some mechanism to control spam for those certificates is found. The authors welcome suggestions.)

documents.title: RFC 6973 excerpt
documents.text: As an example, consider the network access authentication procedures utilizing the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) [RFC3748]. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. To address this threat, as discussed in RFC 4282 [RFC4282], the username part of the NAI (but not the realm part) can be hidden from these eavesdroppers and intermediaries with the cryptographic support offered by EAP methods. Identity confidentiality has become a recommended design criteria for EAP (see [RFC4017]). Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. The EAP method for 3rd Generation Authentication and Key Agreement (EAP-AKA) [RFC4187], for example, protects the EAP peer's identity against passive adversaries by utilizing temporal identities. The canonical format for date-and-time values with an unknown time zone (usually referring to the notion of local time) uses the time-offset -00:00."; reference "RFC 3339: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps RFC 2579: Textual Conventions for SMIv2 XSD-TYPES: XML Schema Part 2: Datatypes Second Edition"; }

documents.title: RFC 7027 excerpt
documents.text: Implementations of elliptic curve cryptography for TLS may be susceptible to side-channel attacks. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. Particular care should be taken for implementations that internally transform curve points to points on the corresponding "twisted curve", using the map (x',y') = (x*Z^2, y*Z^3) with the coefficient Z specified for that curve in [RFC5639], in order to take advantage of an efficient arithmetic based on the twisted curve's special parameters (A = -3). Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. Although the twisted curve itself offers the same level of security as the corresponding random curve (through mathematical equivalence), an arithmetic based on small curve parameters may be harder to protect against side-

documents.title: RFC 7030 excerpt
documents.text: HTTP redirections (3xx status codes) to the same web origin (see [RFC6454]) SHOULD be handled by the client without user input so long as all applicable security checks (Sections 3.3 and 3.6) have been enforced on the initial connection. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. The client initiates a new TLS connection and performs all applicable security checks when redirected to other web origin servers. Redirections to other web origins require the EST client to obtain user input for non-GET or HEAD requests as specified in [RFC2616]. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. Additionally, if the client has already generated a CSR that includes linking identity and POP information (Section 3.5), then the CSR will need to be recreated to incorporate the tls-unique from the new, redirected session. Note: the key pair need not be regenerated. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. These are processing and interface burdens on the client. EST server administrators are advised to take this into consideration.

documents.title: RFC 7120 excerpt
documents.text: In protocol specifications documented in RFCs, there is often a need to allocate code points for various objects, messages, or other protocol entities so that implementations can interoperate. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. Many of these code point spaces have registries handled by the Internet Assigned Number Authority (IANA). Several IETF policies for IANA allocation of protocol parameters are described in RFC 5226 [RFC5226]. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. Some of them, such as "First Come First Served" or "Expert Review", do not require a formal IETF action before the IANA performs allocation. However, in situations where code points are a scarce resource and/or the IETF community has consensus to retain tight control of the registry content, policies such as "IETF Review" (formerly "IETF Consensus"), or "Standards Action" have been used. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. Such allocation policies present a problem in situations where implementation and/or deployment experience are desired or required before the document becomes an RFC.

documents.title: RFC 7230 excerpt
documents.text: For example, if the Upgrade header field is received in a GET request and the server decides to switch protocols, it first responds with a 101 (Switching Protocols) message in HTTP/1.1 and then immediately follows that with the new protocol's equivalent of a response to a GET on the target resource. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. This allows a connection to be upgraded to protocols with the same semantics as HTTP without the latency cost of an additional round trip. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. A server MUST NOT switch protocols unless the received message semantics can be honored by the new protocol; an OPTIONS request can be honored by any protocol.

documents.title: RFC 7231 excerpt
documents.text: Proper interpretation of a PUT request presumes that the user agent knows which target resource is desired. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. A service that selects a proper URI on behalf of the client, after receiving a state-changing request, SHOULD be implemented using the POST method rather than PUT. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. If the origin server will not make the requested PUT state change to the target resource and instead wishes to have it applied to a different resource, such as when the resource has been moved to a different URI, then the origin server MUST send an appropriate 3xx (Redirection) response; the user agent MAY then make its own decision regarding whether or not to redirect the request.

documents.title: RFC 7233 excerpt
documents.text: The combined response message body consists of the union of partial content ranges in the new response and each of the selected responses. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. If the union consists of the entire range of the representation, then the client MUST process the combined response as if it were a complete 200 (OK) response, including a Content-Length header field that reflects the complete length. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. Otherwise, the client MUST process the set of continuous ranges as one of the following: an incomplete 200 (OK) response if the combined response is a prefix of the representation, a single 206 (Partial Content) response containing a multipart/byteranges body, or multiple 206 (Partial Content) responses, each with one continuous range that is indicated by a Content-Range header field.

documents.title: RFC 7296 excerpt
documents.text: Thus, the major version number in the IKE header indicates the version number of the message, not the highest version number that the transmitter supports. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. If the initiator is capable of speaking versions n, n+1, and n+2, and the responder is capable of speaking versions n and n+1, then they will negotiate speaking n+1, where the initiator will set a flag indicating its ability to speak a higher version. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. If they mistakenly (perhaps through an active attacker sending error messages) negotiate to version n, then both will notice that the other side can support a higher version number, and they MUST break the connection and reconnect using version n+1.

documents.title: RFC 7301 excerpt
documents.text: The ALPN extension is intended to follow the typical design of TLS protocol extensions. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. Specifically, the negotiation is performed entirely within the client/server hello exchange in accordance with the established TLS architecture. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. The "application_layer_protocol_negotiation" ServerHello extension is intended to be definitive for the connection (until the connection is renegotiated) and is sent in plaintext to permit network elements to provide differentiated service for the connection when the TCP or UDP port number is not definitive for the application-layer protocol to be used in the connection. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. By placing ownership of protocol selection on the server, ALPN facilitates scenarios in which certificate selection or connection rerouting may be based on the negotiated protocol.

documents.title: RFC 7435 excerpt
documents.text: The Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) model employed by browsers to authenticate web servers (often called the "Web PKI") imposes cost and management burdens that have limited its use. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. With so many Certification Authorities (CAs), not all of which everyone is willing to trust, the communicating parties don't always agree on a mutually trusted CA. Without a mutually trusted CA, authentication fails, leading to communications failure in protocols that mandate authentication. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. These issues are compounded by operational difficulties. For example, a common problem is for site operators to forget to perform timely renewal of expiring certificates. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. In Web PKI interactive applications, security warnings are all too frequent, and end users learn to actively ignore security problems, or site administrators decide that the maintenance cost is not worth the benefit so they provide a cleartext-only service to their users.

documents.title: RFC 7457 excerpt
documents.text: Similarly, there are attacks on the transition between unprotected and TLS-protected traffic. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. A number of IETF application protocols have used an application-level command, usually STARTTLS, to upgrade a cleartext connection to use TLS. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. Multiple implementations of STARTTLS had a flaw where an application-layer input buffer retained commands that were pipelined with the STARTTLS command, such that commands received prior to TLS negotiation are executed after TLS negotiation. This problem is resolved by requiring the application- level command input buffer to be empty before negotiating TLS. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. Note that this flaw lives in the application layer code and does not impact the TLS protocol directly.

documents.title: RFC 7468 excerpt
documents.text: The type of data encoded is labeled depending on the type label in the "-----BEGIN " line (pre-encapsulation boundary). Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. For example, the line may be "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----" to indicate that the content is a PKIX certificate (see further below). Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. Generators MUST put the same label on the "-----END " line (post-encapsulation boundary) as the corresponding "-----BEGIN " line. Labels are formally case-sensitive, uppercase, and comprised of zero or more characters; they do not contain consecutive spaces or hyphen-minuses, nor do they contain spaces or hyphen-minuses at either end. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. Parsers MAY disregard the label in the post-encapsulation boundary instead of signaling an error if there is a label mismatch: some extant implementations require the labels to match; others do not.

documents.title: RFC 7469 excerpt
documents.text: Therefore, there is a necessary trade-off between two competing goods: pin specificity and maximal reduction of the scope of issuers on the one hand; and flexibility and resilience of the host's cryptographic identity on the other hand. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. One way to resolve this trade-off is to compromise by pinning to the key(s) of the issuer(s) of the host's end-entity certificate(s). Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. Often, a valid certificate chain will have at least two certificates above the end-entity certificate: the intermediate issuer and the trust anchor. Operators can pin any one or more of the public keys in this chain, and indeed MUST pin to issuers not in the chain (as, for example, a Backup Pin). Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. Pinning to an intermediate issuer, or even to a trust anchor or root, still significantly reduces the number of issuers who can issue end- entity certificates for the Known Pinned Host, while still giving that host flexibility to change keys without a disruption of service.

documents.title: RFC 7507 excerpt
documents.text: Section 4 does not require client implementations to send TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV in any particular case, it merely recommends it; behavior can be adapted according to the client's security needs. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. It is important to remember that omitting TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV enables downgrade attacks, so implementors must take into account whether the protocol version given by ClientHello.client_version still provides an acceptable level of protection. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. For example, during the initial deployment of a new protocol version (when some interoperability problems may have to be expected), smoothly falling back to the previous protocol version in case of problems may be preferable to potentially not being able to connect at all: so TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV could be omitted for this particular protocol downgrade step.

documents.title: RFC 7515 excerpt
documents.text: The "alg" (algorithm) Header Parameter identifies the cryptographic algorithm used to secure the JWS. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. The JWS Signature value is not valid if the "alg" value does not represent a supported algorithm or if there is not a key for use with that algorithm associated with the party that digitally signed or MACed the content. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. "alg" values should either be registered in the IANA "JSON Web Signature and Encryption Algorithms" registry established by [JWA] or be a value that contains a Collision-Resistant Name. The "alg" value is a case- sensitive ASCII string containing a StringOrURI value. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. This Header Parameter MUST be present and MUST be understood and processed by implementations.

documents.title: RFC 7519 excerpt
documents.text: Support for encrypted JWTs is OPTIONAL. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. If an implementation provides encryption capabilities, of the encryption algorithms specified in [JWA], only RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 with 2048-bit keys ("RSA1_5"), AES Key Wrap with 128- and 256-bit keys ("A128KW" and "A256KW"), and the composite authenticated encryption algorithm using AES-CBC and HMAC SHA-2 ("A128CBC-HS256" and "A256CBC-HS512") MUST be implemented by conforming implementations. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. It is RECOMMENDED that implementations also support using Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral Static (ECDH-ES) to agree upon a key used to wrap the Content Encryption Key ("ECDH-ES+A128KW" and "ECDH-ES+A256KW") and AES in Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) with 128- and 256-bit keys ("A128GCM" and "A256GCM"). Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. Support for other algorithms and key sizes is OPTIONAL.

documents.title: RFC 7525 excerpt
documents.text: Rationale: Cipher suites that offer between 112-bits and 128-bits of security are not considered weak at this time; however, it is expected that their useful lifespan is short enough to justify supporting stronger cipher suites at this time. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. 128-bit ciphers are expected to remain secure for at least several years, and 256-bit ciphers until the next fundamental technology breakthrough. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. Note that, because of so-called "meet-in-the- middle" attacks [Multiple-Encryption], some legacy cipher suites (e.g., 168-bit 3DES) have an effective key length that is smaller than their nominal key length (112 bits in the case of 3DES). Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. Such cipher suites should be evaluated according to their effective key length.

documents.title: RFC 7540 excerpt
documents.text: A client that is unable to retry requests loses all requests that are in flight when the server closes the connection. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. This is especially true for intermediaries that might not be serving clients using HTTP/2. A server that is attempting to gracefully shut down a connection SHOULD send an initial GOAWAY frame with the last stream identifier set to 2^31-1 and a NO_ERROR code. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. This signals to the client that a shutdown is imminent and that initiating further requests is prohibited. After allowing time for any in-flight stream creation (at least one round-trip time), the server can send another GOAWAY frame with an updated last stream identifier. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. This ensures that a connection can be cleanly shut down without losing requests.

documents.title: RFC 7616 excerpt
documents.text: This parameter MUST be used by all implementations. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. The nc parameter stands for "nonce count". The nc value is the hexadecimal count of the number of requests (including the current request) that the client has sent with the nonce value in this request. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. For example, in the first request sent in response to a given nonce value, the client sends "nc=00000001". The purpose of this parameter is to allow the server to detect request replays by maintaining its own copy of this count -- if the same nc value is seen twice, then the request is a replay. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. See the description below of the construction of the response value.

documents.title: RFC 7627 excerpt
documents.text: Synchronization of the "verify_data" in abbreviated handshakes also undermines the security guarantees of the renegotiation indication extension [RFC5746], re-enabling a prefix-injection flaw similar to the renegotiation attack [Ray09]. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. However, in a triple handshake attack, the client sees the server certificate changing across different full handshakes. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. Hence, a precondition to mount this stage of the attack is that the client accepts different certificates at each handshake, even if their common names do not match. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. Before the triple handshake attack was discovered, this used to be widespread behavior, at least among some web browsers; such browsers were hence vulnerable to the attack.

documents.title: RFC 7633 excerpt
documents.text: The OCSP stapling mechanism described in [RFC6066] permits a TLS server to provide evidence of valid certificate status in-band. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. When this information is provided in-band, the privacy, performance, and reliability concerns arising from the need to make a third-party connection during the TLS handshake are eliminated. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. However, a client cannot draw any conclusion from the absence of in-band status information unless it knows that the legitimate server would have provided it. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. The status information might have been omitted because the server does not support the extension or because the server is withholding the information intentionally, knowing the certificate to be invalid.

documents.title: RFC 7641 excerpt
documents.text: To make sure it has a current representation and/or to re-register its interest in a resource, a client MAY issue a new GET request with the same token as the original at any time. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. All options MUST be identical to those in the original request except for the set of ETag Options. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. It is RECOMMENDED that the client does not issue the request while it still has a fresh notification/response for the resource in its cache. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. Additionally, the client SHOULD at least wait for a random amount of time between 5 and 15 seconds after Max-Age expired to reduce collisions with other clients.

documents.title: RFC 7672 excerpt
documents.text: In the absence of DNS lookup errors (Section 2.1.1), if the MX RRset is not "insecure", then it is "secure", and the SMTP client MUST treat each MX hostname as described in Section 2.2.2. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. When, for a given MX hostname, no TLSA records are found or only "insecure" TLSA records are found, DANE TLSA is not applicable with the SMTP server in question, and delivery proceeds to that host as with pre-DANE opportunistic TLS. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. To avoid downgrade attacks, any errors during TLSA lookups MUST, as explained in Section 2.1.2, cause the SMTP server in question to be treated as unreachable.

documents.title: RFC 7685 excerpt

documents.title: RFC 7748 excerpt
documents.text: This memo specifies two elliptic curves ("curve25519" and "curve448") that lend themselves to constant-time implementation and an exception-free scalar multiplication that is resistant to a wide range of side-channel attacks, including timing and cache attacks. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. They are Montgomery curves (where v^2 = u^3 + A*u^2 + u) and thus have birationally equivalent Edwards versions. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. Edwards curves support the fastest (currently known) complete formulas for the elliptic-curve group operations, specifically the Edwards curve x^2 + y^2 = 1 + d*x^2*y^2 for primes p when p = 3 mod 4, and the twisted Edwards curve -x^2 + y^2 = 1 + d*x^2*y^2 when p = 1 mod 4. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. The maps to/from the Montgomery curves to their (twisted) Edwards equivalents are also given.

documents.title: RFC 7761 excerpt
documents.text: Before an interface goes down or changes primary IP address, a Hello message with a zero HoldTime SHOULD be sent immediately (with the old IP address if the IP address changed). Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. This will cause PIM neighbors to remove this neighbor (or its old IP address) immediately. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. After an interface has changed its IP address, it MUST send a Hello message with its new IP address. If an interface changes one of its secondary IP addresses, a Hello message with an updated Address List option and a non-zero HoldTime SHOULD be sent immediately. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. This will cause PIM neighbors to update this neighbor's list of secondary addresses immediately.

documents.title: RFC 7831 excerpt
documents.text: IETF security mechanisms typically take a host name and perhaps a service, entered by a user, and make some trust decision about whether the remote party in the interaction is the intended party. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. This decision can be made via the use of certificates, preconfigured key information, or a previous leap of trust. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. GSS-API has defined a relatively flexible naming convention; however, most of the IETF applications that use GSS-API (including SSH, NFS, IMAP, LDAP, and XMPP) have chosen to use a more restricted naming convention based on the host name. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. The GSS-EAP mechanism needs to support host-based service names in order to work with existing IETF protocols.

documents.title: RFC 7905 excerpt
documents.text: Introduction . ChaCha20 Cipher Suites . Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. IANA Considerations . Security Considerations . Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. References . Normative References . Informative References . Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. 6 Acknowledgements . 8 Authors' Addresses .

documents.title: RFC 7906 excerpt
documents.text: The Enumerated Tag is composed of one or more non-negative integers. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. Each non-negative integer represents a non-hierarchical security attribute that applies to the labeled content. A security policy might define a large set of security categories attributes, but a particular key package generally contains only a few security categories attributes. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. In this case, use of the integer representation is intended to minimize the size of the label. Security attributes enumerated by tags of this type could be restrictive (such as compartments) or permissive (such as release permissions). Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. Two object identifiers for the SecurityCategory type field have been defined, one for restrictive and one for permissive. The object identifiers are:

documents.title: RFC 7919 excerpt
documents.text: However, the ClientHello also contains a list of desired cipher suites, also ranked in preference order. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. This presents the possibility of conflicted preferences. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. For example, if the ClientHello contains a cipher_suite field with two choices in order <TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA> and the Supported Groups extension contains two choices in order <secp256r1,ffdhe3072>, then there is a clear contradiction. Clients SHOULD NOT present such a contradiction since it does not represent a sensible ordering. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. A server that encounters such a contradiction when selecting between an ECDHE or FFDHE key exchange mechanism while trying to respect client preferences SHOULD give priority to the Supported Groups extension (in the example case, it should select TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA with secp256r1) but MAY resolve the contradiction any way it sees fit.

documents.title: RFC 7924 excerpt
documents.text: The purpose of the fingerprint provided by the client is to help the server select the correct information. For example, in case of a Certificate message, the fingerprint identifies the server certificate (and the corresponding private key) for use with the rest of the handshake. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. Servers may have more than one certificate, and therefore a hash needs to be long enough to keep the probably of hash collisions low. On the other hand, the cached info design aims to reduce the amount of data being exchanged. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. The security of the handshake depends on the private key and not on the size of the fingerprint. Hence, the fingerprint is a way to prevent the server from accidentally selecting the wrong information. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. If an attacker injects an incorrect fingerprint, then two outcomes are possible: (1) the fingerprint does not relate to any cached state and the server has to fall back to a full exchange, and (2) if the attacker manages to inject a fingerprint that refers to data the client has not cached, then the exchange will fail later when the client continues with the handshake and aims to verify the digital signature. The signature verification will fail since the public key cached by the client will not correspond to the private key that was used by the server to sign the message.

documents.title: RFC 7932 excerpt
documents.text: At any given point during decoding the compressed data, a reference to a duplicated string in the uncompressed data produced so far has a maximum backward distance value, which is the minimum of the window size and the number of uncompressed bytes produced. Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. However, decoding a distance from the compressed stream, as described in Section 4, can produce distances that are greater than this maximum allowed value. Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. In this case, the distance is treated as a reference to a word in the static dictionary given in Appendix A. The copy length for a static dictionary reference must be between 4 and 24. Conformant implementations SHALL exhibit auditable behavior for every event covered by this section. The static dictionary has three parts:

documents.title: RFC 7942 excerpt
documents.text: Introduction . The "Implementation Status" Section . Auditable evidence MUST be retained for the period mandated by the deploying jurisdiction. Introductory Text . Alternative Formats . Non-conformant behavior MUST be surfaced through the designated fault channel without delay. Security Considerations . Informative References .
